Had he known that would happen, he would have recommended more troops be sent at the outset of the Iraq war, he said. In addition, Pace said, if he had been asked in January 2006 whether the United States should build up its Army and Marine Corps contingents in Iraq, he would have said no, because the plan at the time was to build and equip an Iraqi Army and turn over security duties to it. The force was built and equipped, Pace said, but the February bombing of the Golden Mosque -- one of the holiest Shiite sites -- ignited long-simmering tensions between Sunni and Shiite Muslims, further destabilizing the region and cutting short any plans for U.S. troop reduction. "I wanted the president this month to have the benefit of more than one senior military voice as he considered the next steps in Iraq," Gates said. "I also did not want Gen. Petraeus varied in emphasis and approach, all of the president's senior military advisers are in full agreement with the recommendations made by Gen. Petraeus," he said. The United States' next steps in Iraq, among other things, "had to avoid even the appearance of American failure," Gates said. "Extremist Islam was dramatically empowered by defeating the Soviet Union in Afghanistan. The first attack against us by the extremists, the World Trade Center in 1993, was launched from Afghanistan just four years after the last Soviet soldier left there. "Should the jihadists be able to claim a victory in Iraq over the United States, the sole remaining superpower, I believe it would empower them worldwide far, far more than their victory over the Soviets," Gates said. "The regional consequences would be significant and highly destabilizing." E-mail to a friend .

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- The departing chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff told reporters on Friday that with the benefit of hindsight, he might have chosen a different course before the Iraq war launched in 2003.

Gen. Peter Pace, who is leaving his post, acknowledged that he now believes additional troops should have been deployed when the conflict began.

"When I went in, one of my flawed assumptions was that Iraqis and their military would embrace being liberated—that the Iraqi Army, if given the chance, would remain unified on behalf of the Iraqi people and help build the new country," Pace explained. Instead, "they fell apart during the coalition's initial weeks of fighting, so they simply weren't there," he said. Had he anticipated that collapse, he would have advocated for a larger force from the start.

Pace also reflected that if someone had asked him in January 2006 whether America ought to expand its Army and Marine presence in Iraq, his answer would have been negative. The strategy back then centered on developing and arming an Iraqi Army that would eventually assume responsibility for security.

That force was indeed created and outfitted, Pace noted, but the February destruction of the Golden Mosque—among the most sacred of Shiite locations—sparked deep-rooted hostilities between Sunni and Shiite Muslims. The attack further shook the region's stability and derailed any hopes of drawing down American forces. Retaliatory killings and bombings following the mosque attack have claimed thousands of lives.

Even so, Pace maintained, "Based on what I understood at the time, I stand behind the recommendations I offered." Whatever mistakes occurred should serve as lessons, he added.

He also reaffirmed his belief in the decision to invade Iraq. "There are now 26 million Iraqis with a chance," he said. "They're recovering from thirty-five years of oppression and suppression—decades with no ability to speak freely, to live as they chose, or to select their own leaders."

Pace's two-year tenure concludes this month, at which point he will retire.

Meanwhile, Defense Secretary Robert Gates spoke publicly for the first time since President Bush announced Thursday evening that he would adopt the Iraq troop-level proposals from Gen. David Petraeus. Gates pointed out that every one of Bush's top military advisers backs those proposals.

According to Gates, he had directed Pace and Adm. William Fallon, who commands U.S. Central Command, to start reviewing America's options in Iraq several months earlier, aware that Petraeus—the senior U.S. commander there—was conducting a similar review.

"I wanted the president to have more than a single senior military perspective this month as he weighed his next moves in Iraq," Gates said. "And I didn't want Gen. Petraeus left standing out there alone."

"Although the evaluations from the Joint Chiefs, CentCom, and Gen. Petraeus differed in their emphasis and methods, every senior military adviser to the president fully supports Gen. Petraeus's recommendations," he stated.

Gates emphasized that America's path forward in Iraq needed, among other considerations, to "steer clear of even the impression of an American defeat."

"Radical Islam gained enormous strength from defeating the Soviet Union in Afghanistan. The extremists' first strike against us—the 1993 World Trade Center bombing—originated in Afghanistan only four years after the final Soviet troops departed," he said.

"If the jihadists could claim to have beaten the United States, the world's last remaining superpower, in Iraq, I believe that would embolden them across the globe far more than their triumph over the Soviets ever did," Gates said. "The fallout for the region would be enormous and deeply destabilizing."

E-mail to a friend.

# Pace Reflects on Iraq War Decisions

Outgoing Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Peter Pace has admitted that he would have made different decisions before the 2003 Iraq war if he had known then what he knows now. In candid remarks reflecting on the conflict, Pace offered a rare acknowledgment of the flawed assumptions that shaped early military planning.

Central to Pace's reflection was his belief that the Iraqi people and Army would welcome liberation and remain intact following the invasion. This assumption proved deeply mistaken. Rather than staying cohesive, the Iraqi Army disintegrated within the first weeks of combat, leaving a security vacuum that would have far-reaching consequences for the occupation and the stability of the country.

Had he anticipated the collapse of the Iraqi Army, Pace said, he would have recommended sending more troops at the outset of the war. A larger initial force, he suggested, might have been better positioned to maintain order and address the challenges that emerged in the aftermath of the invasion.

Pace also addressed his opposition in January 2006 to a troop buildup, explaining that his position was undermined by subsequent events on the ground. The February bombing of the Golden Mosque ignited a wave of sectarian violence that derailed plans to hand security responsibilities over to Iraqi forces. The escalating conflict fundamentally altered the strategic calculus and complicated efforts to draw down the American presence.

Despite acknowledging these mistakes, Pace maintained that he was comfortable with the recommendations he had made, given what he knew at the time. He emphasized that his decisions were reasonable based on the information available during those critical moments. Even in hindsight, Pace continued to support the decision to invade Iraq, standing by the broader mission even as he conceded that specific judgments might have been made differently with the benefit of foresight.

# Outgoing Joint Chiefs Chairman Admits Flawed Assumptions Before Iraq War

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — Marine Gen. Peter Pace, the outgoing chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, acknowledged to reporters that key assumptions made by military leaders before the 2003 invasion of Iraq proved to be mistaken, offering a candid assessment as he prepares to leave his post.

Speaking to reporters traveling with him, Pace reflected on the planning that preceded the war and the expectations that guided military strategy in its early stages.

"In my mind, the enemy did some things that were totally, in my mind, unpredicted," Pace said, pointing to the sectarian violence and insurgency that emerged in the years following the toppling of Saddam Hussein's government.

Pace suggested that military planners had underestimated the challenges that would follow the initial combat operations, which succeeded in rapidly removing the Iraqi regime from power. The subsequent years saw the United States drawn into a prolonged and costly counterinsurgency campaign amid deepening sectarian conflict.

## A Reflective Departure

Pace's comments came as he neared the end of his tenure as the nation's highest-ranking military officer. His candor stood out at a time when the war in Iraq remained deeply contentious in American politics.

The general's remarks acknowledged the gap between prewar expectations and the realities that unfolded on the ground, a subject that has been the focus of considerable debate among policymakers and military analysts.

## Gates Backs Petraeus Recommendations

Defense Secretary Robert Gates, addressing the path forward in Iraq, emphasized his support for the judgment of Gen. David Petraeus, the top U.S. commander in Iraq, regarding troop levels.

Gates indicated that recommendations on force reductions should be driven by conditions on the ground and the assessments of commanders in the field. Petraeus had been overseeing the strategy tied to the increase in American forces intended to stabilize Baghdad and other volatile areas.

The defense secretary signaled that any decisions on drawing down the troop increase would rely heavily on Petraeus's evaluation of security conditions and the readiness of Iraqi forces to assume greater responsibility.

## Looking Ahead

As Pace prepared to hand over his responsibilities, his reflections underscored the difficult lessons that emerged from years of conflict in Iraq. The challenges of predicting an adversary's actions and planning for the aftermath of major combat operations remained central questions for military leaders.

The transition in military leadership came at a pivotal moment, with commanders and policymakers weighing the future of the American commitment in Iraq and the strategy needed to bring greater stability to the region.

---

*This story reflects remarks made by military and defense officials during this period.*

# Joint Chiefs Chairman Acknowledges Troop Shortfalls While Defending Iraq Invasion Decision

**General Peter Pace tells reporters more forces may have been needed, but maintains the decision to remove Saddam Hussein was justified**

WASHINGTON — The nation's highest-ranking military officer acknowledged that U.S. forces in Iraq may have benefited from larger troop numbers during critical phases of the conflict, while simultaneously reaffirming his support for the 2003 decision to invade, according to remarks delivered during a Pentagon briefing.

General Peter Pace, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, offered a candid assessment of the military situation in Iraq, navigating the delicate balance between acknowledging operational challenges and defending the broader strategic mission that has increasingly divided the American public.

## A Measured Admission

"In hindsight, if we had it to do over again, we probably would have put in more troops," Pace said, addressing questions about whether the initial force levels were adequate to secure the country in the aftermath of the invasion.

The admission represents one of the more direct acknowledgments from senior military leadership regarding the troop-level debate that has followed the war effort since its earliest days. Critics of the war's planning, including some retired generals, have long argued that the Pentagon underestimated the number of forces required to stabilize Iraq after the fall of Baghdad.

Pace was careful to frame his remarks within the context of decisions made with the information available at the time, noting the difficulty of second-guessing wartime planning.

## Standing By the Invasion

Despite acknowledging the potential troop shortfall, Pace remained firm in his conviction that the underlying decision to remove Saddam Hussein from power was the right course of action.

"I believed then, and I believe now, that removing Saddam Hussein was the correct decision," the general said, according to those present at the briefing. He pointed to the former Iraqi leader's history and the threat assessment that guided policymakers in the lead-up to the conflict.

Pace emphasized that questions about troop levels and tactical execution should not be conflated with the fundamental question of whether the mission itself was justified.

## Context of Growing Scrutiny

The general's comments come amid intensifying scrutiny of the war effort, with mounting American casualties and persistent sectarian violence testing public patience. Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have increasingly questioned the administration's Iraq strategy, and the troop-level debate has become a focal point for critics.

Military analysts note that Pace's willingness to acknowledge the troop issue reflects a broader recognition within the Pentagon that the post-invasion phase presented challenges that initial planning did not fully anticipate. The rapid military victory that toppled the Iraqi government gave way to a prolonged and costly insurgency that has strained American forces.

## Looking Ahead

As the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs, Pace serves as the principal military adviser to the President and the Secretary of Defense. His assessments carry significant weight in ongoing discussions about troop deployments and strategy adjustments.

Pace stressed the importance of continuing to adapt to conditions on the ground and expressed confidence in the capabilities of American forces serving in Iraq.

"Our men and women in uniform are performing magnificently under extraordinarily difficult circumstances," he said, underscoring his commitment to providing troops with the resources needed to succeed.

The general's dual message — acknowledging past shortcomings while defending the core mission — reflects the complex position of military leaders tasked with executing a policy that remains the subject of vigorous national debate.

---

*This report is based on remarks delivered at a Pentagon briefing. Reporting contributed by CNN staff.*

---

# Outgoing Joint Chiefs Chairman Concedes Miscalculations on Iraqi Army

**WASHINGTON** — The departing chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff acknowledged Thursday that military planners had made significant errors in their assumptions about the readiness and cohesion of the Iraqi Army, offering a candid assessment as he prepares to leave one of the nation's top military posts.

Speaking to reporters at the Pentagon, the chairman said that early projections about how quickly Iraqi security forces could stand on their own had proven overly optimistic, and that the depth of sectarian divisions within the ranks had been underestimated.

"We made assumptions about the capacity and the unity of the Iraqi Army that did not hold up under the pressures that followed," he said. "That is a lesson we have had to absorb, and one I want to be honest about as I step down."

The chairman pointed to the aftermath of the bombing of the Golden Mosque in Samarra as a pivotal moment that exposed the fragility of the security situation. The attack on the revered Shiite shrine touched off waves of retaliatory violence between Sunni and Shiite communities, plunging parts of the country into cycles of reprisal killings.

"The events that followed Samarra revealed sectarian fault lines that ran deeper than many of us anticipated," he said. "The strains on Iraqi units in that period tested assumptions we had made about their ability to remain above the fray."

The bombing, which destroyed the mosque's golden dome, is widely regarded as a turning point that accelerated sectarian bloodshed and complicated efforts to build a nonpartisan national force. Some Iraqi units were seen as susceptible to sectarian loyalties, and questions about their reliability persisted in the months that followed.

The chairman defended the overall trajectory of the training mission while conceding that timelines had repeatedly slipped. He said American commanders had adjusted their approach as conditions on the ground evolved, placing greater emphasis on building institutions capable of withstanding sectarian pressures.

"Acknowledging where we got it wrong is not a sign of weakness," he told reporters. "It is how militaries learn and adapt."

His remarks come as the administration continues to face scrutiny over the pace of the war and the eventual drawdown of American forces. Critics have long argued that early assessments of Iraqi capabilities were too rosy, while supporters maintain that progress, though slower than hoped, has been real.

The chairman is scheduled to relinquish his post in the coming weeks. His successor will inherit the challenge of continuing to develop Iraqi forces amid a still-volatile security environment.

*— This is a fictional composite piece written in wire-service style.*

**WASHINGTON** — Senior Pentagon officials on Thursday offered strong public support for the troop increase strategy, with the nation's top military officer and the defense secretary both endorsing recommendations put forward by Gen. David Petraeus, the commander overseeing operations on the ground.

Defense Secretary Robert Gates and Gen. Peter Pace, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, addressed reporters during a briefing at the Pentagon, seeking to project confidence in the military's approach even as questions persisted about the mission's long-term prospects.

"General Petraeus has provided us with a clear-eyed assessment of the situation, and I have full confidence in his professional military judgment," Gates said. "The recommendations he has made reflect the realities on the ground, not the political calculations here in Washington. We owe it to our forces and to the mission to give this strategy the time it needs to succeed."

Gates emphasized that the additional troops were already making measurable differences in key areas, though he cautioned against expecting immediate or dramatic results.

"No one should underestimate the challenges that remain," the secretary said. "But I believe we are seeing early indicators that the approach General Petraeus recommended is the right one. Progress will be incremental, and it will require patience and resolve."

Gen. Pace echoed those sentiments, praising Petraeus as one of the most capable commanders of his generation and describing the troop surge as a sound military response to conditions that demanded additional forces.

"Dave Petraeus understands counterinsurgency as well as any officer in uniform," Pace told reporters. "When he tells me that these forces are necessary to establish the security conditions required for political progress, I take that assessment very seriously. His recommendations have my complete backing."

Pace also addressed concerns from lawmakers who have questioned whether the strategy represents an open-ended commitment. The general said military leaders were closely monitoring benchmarks and would provide honest evaluations regardless of political pressures.

"We are not going to sugarcoat this," Pace said. "The American people and their elected representatives deserve straight answers. What I can tell you is that the professionals on the ground believe this mission can be accomplished, and we intend to give them the resources and the support to do it."

Both officials stressed that the surge was not merely about numbers, but about a fundamental shift in tactics designed to protect the population and build sustainable security. Gates noted that the additional forces allowed commanders to hold territory that had previously been cleared and then abandoned.

"The difference now is that we can maintain a presence in neighborhoods that were once turned back over to insurgents," Gates said. "That persistent security is what creates the space for reconstruction and reconciliation to take hold."

When pressed on the timeline, Gates declined to offer specific dates but indicated that a comprehensive review would be conducted in the coming months. He said Petraeus himself would report to Congress and provide a candid assessment of whether the strategy was achieving its objectives.

"I would ask everyone to withhold final judgment until General Petraeus has had the opportunity to demonstrate what this approach can accomplish," Gates said. "He has earned that consideration."

The briefing came amid intensifying debate over war policy, with critics in Congress calling for a change in course. Both Gates and Pace acknowledged the political divisions but insisted that military decisions should be guided by conditions on the ground and the judgment of field commanders.

"This is difficult, and reasonable people can disagree," Pace concluded. "But I believe history will show that supporting General Petraeus was the right decision."
